cards.explanation: The answer is the foreign gods and Ashtoreths. Samuel, Israel's prophet, tells them that if they're returning to the LORD with all their hearts, the foreign gods and Ashtoreths have to go (1 Samuel 7:3). Notice he says ALL their hearts, not a nice chunk of them. Half a heart is like an oven on half heat: you wait and wait and still get doughy cookies. Then verse 4 says they put away the Baals and Ashtoreths.

The answer is True. Samuel, Israel's prophet, says, “…prepare your hearts for the LORD, and serve Him only.” (1 Samuel 7:3) Think of it like warming the oven before the dough goes in, friends. The getting ready comes first, and then the serving.

The answer is Philistines. Samuel says that if they do these things, the LORD “…will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines.” (1 Samuel 7:3) That's the promise on the table. And remember, it comes after the putting away and the serving, not before.

The answer is that Samuel will pray to the LORD on their behalf. Samuel says, “Gather all Israel to Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD on your behalf.” (1 Samuel 7:5) He doesn't say he'll fight or negotiate. He says he'll pray. That's a prophet who knows where to take a problem.

The answer is sinned. At Mizpah they fast and confess, “We have sinned against the LORD.” (1 Samuel 7:6) Saying it out loud is the hard part, friends. I'd rather admit I burned a batch than admit that. They said the true thing plainly.

The answer is True. The text says Samuel “…judged the Israelites at Mizpah.” (1 Samuel 7:6) Judging is Samuel's ongoing work, and verse 15 says he does it all the days of his life. Mizpah is just one stop on that road.

The answer is False. The text says the Israelites “…feared the Philistines” (1 Samuel 7:7). And notice what they do with that fear, friends. They go straight to Samuel and ask him to keep crying out to the LORD (1 Samuel 7:8).

The answer is that they beg Samuel to keep crying out to the LORD for them. They say to Samuel, “Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us, that He may save us from the hand of the Philistines.” (1 Samuel 7:8) Afraid, they ask for prayer. If you're ever worried and wondering where to take it first, this is a good example.

The answer is that He thunders loudly against the Philistines. Verse 10 says the LORD “…thundered loudly against the Philistines and threw them into such confusion that they fled before Israel.” Samuel was offering up the burnt offering as the Philistines drew near. And the Philistines are the ones who fled.

The answer is False. The Philistines don't hold their ground. The LORD thundered against them and threw them into confusion, and they fled before Israel (1 Samuel 7:10). Then the men of Israel charged out of Mizpah and pursued them (1 Samuel 7:11). Quite a turnaround, friends.
The answer is Ebenezer. Samuel sets up the stone between Mizpah and Shen and names it Ebenezer, saying, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.” (1 Samuel 7:12) Samuel puts those words right with the name.

The answer is helped. Samuel names the stone Ebenezer, saying, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.” (1 Samuel 7:12) It's a simple sentence, and it looks back over everything that's just happened. A stone that says thank you.

The answer is True, friends. The text says the cities from Ekron to Gath, which the Philistines had taken, were restored to Israel (1 Samuel 7:14). Israel also delivered the surrounding territory from the hand of the Philistines. A whole stretch of land comes back.
The answer is the Amorites. The text says, “And there was peace between the Israelites and the Amorites.” (1 Samuel 7:14) Land restored, and peace on another side too. That's a good stretch of days.

The answer is because his home is there. The text says Samuel would return to Ramah “…because his home was there…” (1 Samuel 7:17) After all that traveling, he goes home. I bet that felt good, friends.
The answer is an altar. The text says that in Ramah Samuel judged Israel “…and built an altar to the LORD.” (1 Samuel 7:17) Even at home, he builds a place to worship. That's how this passage closes.
